content: 1. Social and financial risk protection is essential to ensure equitable access to healthcare services, regardless of an individual's socioeconomic status. Improved efficiency in healthcare systems can enhance service delivery and responsiveness to patient needs. 2. Service delivery in healthcare is directly influenced by the inputs into the system, such as the health workforce, procurement of medical supplies, and financing. Increasing these inputs should lead to better service delivery and improved access to healthcare services. 3. A key function of a health system is to ensure the availability and accessibility of healthcare services that meet or exceed minimum quality standards. These services should be organized around the needs and preferences of individuals, rather than being dictated by the disease or the individual's ability to pay. 4. Healthcare services must be perceived as responsive and acceptable by users, promoting a model where individuals actively participate in their own healthcare decisions. Continuity of care across various health conditions, service networks, and levels of care is critical throughout an individual's life course. 5. The WHO global competency and outcomes framework for Universal Health Coverage (UHC) emphasizes the competencies required for health workers to deliver promotive, preventive, curative, rehabilitative, and palliative health services. This framework is relevant for both pre-service and in-service education and training. 6. Training for health workers should include communication skills to facilitate informed decision-making, clarification of values, collaborative practice, and empathetic approaches to care. This ensures that care delivery is people-centered, non-judgmental, and supportive of individuals' autonomy in making healthcare decisions. 7. Self-care interventions, even when accessed outside formal health services, require some level of engagement with the health system. Health workers must adopt inclusive and non-stigmatizing attitudes to promote safety, patient safety, and equity. 8. Health workers and healthcare facility managers, whether in the public or private sector, are responsible for delivering services that meet professional ethical standards and internationally agreed human rights principles. They must also recognize and support the role of self-care in holistic health management plans. 9. Health information and services must be available, accessible, acceptable, and of high quality. Reliable and accurate information is essential for individuals to make informed decisions about their health and well-being. 10. Mobile phones, tablets, and other information and communication technologies offer new opportunities to deliver health information. Visual materials, such as pictures, can help overcome language barriers and literacy issues. 11. Patient information leaflets are a legal requirement in many countries and must be designed to ensure that patients can make informed decisions about the safe and effective use of medical products and interventions. 12. Expanding health management information systems to capture data on self-care interventions may be necessary to address the broader scope of healthcare delivery beyond traditional health system boundaries. 13. The regulation of medical products, vaccines, and technologies is critical to ensure their quality, safety, and performance. This includes addressing the risks posed by informal or unregulated vendors supplying products of unknown quality. 14. Transparent and effective accountability mechanisms must be established to ensure that individuals can seek remedy, redress, and justice through the health system. These mechanisms should operate alongside other social accountability systems. 15. Mechanisms must be in place to overcome barriers to the uptake and use of self-care interventions, as well as barriers to continued engagement with the health system. These barriers may occur at individual, interpersonal, community, and societal levels. 16. Strategies are needed across all health system building blocks to improve the availability, accessibility, acceptability, affordability, and equitable coverage of self-care interventions. Addressing these barriers is essential to creating an enabling environment for self-care. 17. The enabling environment for self-care interventions must be conducive to the realization of health and well-being, particularly as these interventions are often accessed outside formal health services. 18. Policies and procedures are needed to ensure that individuals can safely report rights violations, such as discrimination or denial of health services, and seek redress. Access to justice must be facilitated for all individuals, including those using self-care interventions. 19. Economic empowerment, poverty reduction, and access to resources such as housing and food support can improve access to healthcare and health outcomes. These interventions address socioeconomic vulnerabilities that contribute to poor health outcomes. 20. Education, particularly secondary education, is crucial for empowering individuals in their health and well-being. Comprehensive sexuality education (CSE) plays a central role in enabling young people to make informed decisions about their sexuality and relationships. 21. Violence, in its various forms, undermines individuals' ability to make health-promoting decisions and access sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services. Efforts to address violence must involve multiple sectors, including the health sector. 22. Stigma and discrimination create barriers to accessing SRH services and self-care interventions. Protecting against these barriers is essential to ensure equitable access to healthcare for all individuals, particularly those who are marginalized or vulnerable. 23. Special attention must be given to populations at higher risk of stigma, exclusion, and violence, such as people living with HIV, transgender individuals, and those engaged in sex work. Addressing these issues is critical to creating an enabling environment for self-care interventions.
